cause: The pilot box ran out of disk at 08:08-08:09 MSK. Chain, measured: seaweed's two volume servers are at Volumes==Max (4198/4198 and 6912/6912, Topology Free=0 of Max=11110, started with -max=0 -minFreeSpace=5GiB) → seaweed-master logs 'topo failed to pick 1 from 0 node candidates' ~1,500 times per 2 min → seaweed-filer 'retry assign: giving up after 30s' → s3 'putToFiler: chunked upload failed: assign volume: all filers failed' → recorder-service S3UploadFailedError, so recorded segments stay in its container-local /tmp/recorder, which grew at 750 MB/min (22.9→27.1 GB observed) and filled the disk. Both volume servers were simultaneously vacuuming event-clips volumes (9977/9987/10058/13571), which matches the IO storm measured from 07:25 (io full-stall 26-43 %, reads 100-230 MB/s, writes to 280 MB/s). Consequences here: the soak driver died at 08:09:28 writing events.log (OSError 28), `systemctl --user start wt-warden` failed in the same second so the Watchtower supervisor was down until I restarted it at 08:20, and the disk hit 0 free twice
fix: Mine: soak stopped 08:29 (rate unchanged, so the soak is not the driver), warden restarted, disk watchdog armed at an 8 GB floor, soak rows 310-342 of the restarted run kept. CV's: docker image prune (images 49→11, 56.4→36.16 GB) freed 24 GB and bought ~50 min, but did NOT restore assignment because the slot ceiling, not free space, is exhausted — reported to CV with the numbers. Outstanding on CV's side: reclaim inside existing volumes / retention deletion / raise the per-node ceiling. Soak rows measured between 07:25 and 08:09 carry the storm and are flagged in the host-condition section. RESOLVED 09:04 by CV restarting one seaweed volume server (07fa7c7d), which recomputes the -max=0 ceiling at STARTUP: that node went Volumes=4198/Max=4198 (0 free slots) to Max=4307 (109 free), Topology Free 0->109. Confirmed independently from this box: free space bottomed at 14.3 GB then rose ~800 MB/min, the spool drained ~700 MB/min (48.6->45.9 GB), assign errors stopped. So -max=0 is NOT 'unlimited' and does NOT re-derive while running - it recomputes only at startup; CV has owned that two comments in their codebase (capacity.py:49 and :403, storage-agent seaweed_volume.py) assert the opposite. The ceiling moved by 109 with 759 GB free on /data and ~14 GB on /, and neither CV nor I can derive that number from one observation; a second restart at a different / free level would discriminate the inputs. REPRIEVE, NOT CURE: measured consumption is 2 volumes per 3 min while the backlog drains (~0.7/min, ~2.5 h for 100 slots) and nearer 0.3/min at CV's ~20 GB/hour steady state (~5 h). The explicit -max remains the real fix and is the operator's ruling. CV's restart also surfaced two keepers: docker restart FAILED on a zombie main PID ('use the --init option') and left the container exited with 2.8 TB offline until docker start - these containers run without an init, so a restart under load may need stop-then-start - and one volume (raw-video-hot_10516.dat) has a truncated tail from the ENOSPC that SeaweedFS indexed around. My 34 GB Qt scratch was offered but NOT deleted; the restart removed the need. FINAL, after CV restarted the second volume server (4fa8f6a7) once the soak ended: the ceiling formula is ruled out rather than solved, which is the durable result. node 07fa7c7d had 759 GB free on /data and ~14 GB on / and gained 109 slots (4198->4307); node 4fa8f6a7 had 1.4 TB on /data and ~46 GB on / and gained only 47 (6912->6959). MORE free space on either filesystem produced FEWER slots, and it is not proportional to volume count either (2.6 % vs 0.7 %). So: do not reason about seaweed capacity from a guessed formula - restart, then MEASURE Topology Free. Reload time does scale cleanly, ~30 ms per volume (142 s for 4198, 263 s for 6912). Combined free slots 84, about 4 hours at the measured 0.35/min drain; the explicit -max is still the only cure. RUNBOOK, sharpened because the zombie trap repeated on the second node exactly as predicted: `docker restart` uses a 10 s default stop timeout and FAILS on these containers; `docker stop -t 60` followed by `docker start` worked cleanly on both. Shell trap, stated narrowly after BOTH of us checked our repos rather than generalising: `docker restart X 2>&1 | sed ... || fallback` makes `||` test SED's exit status, not docker's, so the fallback silently does not fire. It bit CV's ad-hoc command tonight. It is NOT present in committed code on either side - CV found their four `docker restart`/`docker stop` mentions only PRINT the command for a human, with 48 scripts setting pipefail and every `| sed ... ||` being a deliberate `|| true`; this repo has NO script that runs a container restart at all, its pipe-then-`||` uses are defaults like `|| echo -1`, and 15 of 26 shell scripts set pipefail. So the true statement is: this bites interactive one-liners, and any restart script someone writes later. I had written that it 'would bite any restart script in this repo as easily as in yours' - that was unverified about both repos and is corrected here. If anyone does script a restart, test docker's exit status directly or set pipefail. Final state at hand-back: 46 GB free, spool 936 MB steady, 228 uploads/min with zero failures, recording restored to full fleet (659 segments across 74 cameras in three minutes, against 865 across 71 in the same window a day earlier)

cause: CONFIRMED BY CV from the manifest of the same session (2c351168), with the cause named: the overlap is at a CODEC boundary, not a recording gap. Their manifest read: frag 2 = 23:48:57.000→23:49:15.809 (18.809 s), frag 3 = 23:49:11.000→23:49:15.809 (4.809 s, disc=True, boundary="codec") — frag 3 starts 4.809 s before frag 2's declared end and both end at the same instant. The session is hevc_capable, so the hot window is served as HEVC main and the rest as H.264 sub, and the two renditions declare the SAME 4.809 s of wall time. CV's earlier 0.007 s figure came from a GAP-boundary session (boundary="gap"), where spans are genuinely disjoint — they generalised from the wrong boundary type and have owned that. My three fresh gap-free 60 s sessions (.183/.184/.102, 59.850-59.851 s declared, zero overlapping pairs) are consistent: no codec switch, no overlap. So this is a distinct defect from the edge over-serve: CV now tracks D1 = edge over-serve (fix: trim served bytes to the declared span) and D2 = codec-boundary wall overlap (fix: the manifest must not emit overlapping wall spans across a codec switch). Neither is built; sequencing is the operator's. CONTRACT GAP, from mobile (and a correction of mine — I asserted their rows carried the boundary type without checking): the mobile client's manifest fragment type is wall_start / wall_end / availability only (src/api/vision/client.ts:889), no disc and no boundary. So mobile can DETECT an overlap from intersecting wall spans but cannot NAME the boundary type — the exact distinction that made CV's first measurement miss this. Additive field asked of CV. Mobile also corrected their own earlier account of their failure mode: theirs is not 'lands on whichever copy the player picks', it is a SYSTEMATIC early offset, because their mapping is wall-linear ((wallMs - sessionStartMs)/1000) while the HLS timeline is cumulative EXTINF — so past a codec boundary every target lands ~4.809 s early, in the same direction, compounding with each overlapping boundary. Their reasoning, not measured; a testable prediction for the recipe session
fix: none shipped. CLIENT-SIDE DETECTION IS POSSIBLE TODAY and is the deferred TODO: our fragment rows already carry the boundary type across the C++→QML boundary (PlaybackClient.cpp:436 positional row [cs, ce, wsMs, weMs, disc, boundary, codec, tier, resolution, stream_type]; EvHeroPlayer.qml:880 keeps disc+boundary), so EvHeroPlayer._wallToPos can detect a target that falls inside two fragment spans — and specifically one where the later fragment has boundary=="codec" — and trace it. Detection and trace only at first: which copy holds decodable frames is unmeasured, and a policy chosen on reasoning alone would turn a silent wrong answer into a confident one. Not built tonight because compiling writes object files onto a nearly-full disk. Note our hero already RE-OPENS for a jump that crosses a kept boundary (_crossesBoundary), so the exposure is a seek landing INSIDE the overlapped span, not one crossing it

cause: The recorder's spool leak is not a leak of duplicates - it is silent data loss. 147 files older than today survived tonight's 46 GB drain untouched (161.7 MB, oldest hiwatch-08cc81e5d919/sub/seg-20260908-222917.ts, four days old). CV then checked the catalogue: video_segments rows for that segment's minute = ZERO. So those segments were recorded, failed to upload, were never catalogued, and nothing retries them. Retention will not reap them either, because retention deletes CATALOGUED segments. They are the ONLY copy of that footage and they sit in a container-local /tmp/recorder indefinitely. The consequence that matters operationally: the obvious remediation is the WRONG one. Anyone who frees space during a disk alert by clearing /tmp/recorder destroys real footage permanently - and /tmp/recorder is exactly the 46 GB directory that looks like junk during an alert. CV has it in their incident file in capitals and the correct fix is a retry/reconcile pass that re-uploads and catalogues orphaned spool files, not a cleanup job. UPDATE 09:30, CV: the fuse was shorter than either of us said. The spool lives on the container's WRITABLE LAYER, so `docker compose up --build recorder-service` destroys it - and CV had been rebuilding containers all session. The footage was one routine deploy from gone, not one disk-alert rm.
fix: PRESERVED by CV: /mnt/cilex-storage/orphaned-spool/2026-09-12/orphans.tar.gz, 147 files, 139.9 MB, verified by listing the archive, on the data disk rather than the container layer. Copied not moved, originals left in place, with a README beside it recording what they are, that they have zero video_segments rows, and what restoring them needs. Our two client-side constraints were taken as REQUIREMENTS for the future reconcile pass and the second travels in that README: (1) idempotent and safe against a spool being written concurrently, because the moment it is useful is exactly when uploads are failing and the directory is growing; (2) rows must carry the TRUE recorded timestamps parsed from seg-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.ts, never upload time - four-day-old footage catalogued as today puts a guard's evening in the wrong place on the scrubber, which is worse than it being missing, and is the test to write before shipping. Nothing to change on our side: our client reads the catalogue and shows an honest empty state for that minute, which is correct given what the system knows and is exactly why nobody noticed.

cause: The defect behind tonight's outage is not 'the recorder spool leaks' - it is APPLICATION DATA WRITTEN TO CONTAINER WRITABLE LAYERS. The spool was simply the instance large enough to take the box down; any other instance is invisible until a rebuild eats it, and rebuilds are routine. Two instances known so far. (1) recorder-service /tmp/recorder: the live spool, 46 GB at peak, and 147 files in it were the ONLY copy of real footage (zero video_segments rows) - preserved by CV to /mnt/cilex-storage/orphaned-spool/2026-09-12/ (139.9 MB, copied not moved, README beside it). (2) query-api /tmp/cilex-event-stills, 83 MB, 2,563 entries - flagged by this box from a measurement taken while hunting the disk filler, checked by CV (routers/events.py:1138): these are a CACHE of JPEG frames pulled from recorded segments, so they regenerate and losing the layer costs CPU, not data. BENIGN TODAY, TWO LATENT BUGS: there is no eviction, TTL or size cap on that directory, so it only grows; and it is young only because query-api is redeployed often (CV wiped it several times today without noticing). In a stable deployment it grows unbounded on the root disk and eventually holds stills whose source footage has passed retention - at which point those JPEGs become the only copy, on a layer a rebuild destroys. Same shape as the spool, arriving later and quieter.
fix: Nothing for us to change; both instances are CV's. Recorded here because the generalisation is the transferable part and because the next person meeting a full disk on this box needs it before they reach for rm or a rebuild. CV has taken the framing as the heading of their incident file and noted that their other services want auditing for the same shape. Neither latent bug is urgent, neither is fixed.

cause: Post-incident backend catch-up, NOT the cold-window class of the earlier rollover outliers: the SESSION CREATE was slow (session_http 1,262-2,258 ms against the 50-750 ms seen all night, session_ready 1,269 ms) while segment serves were normal (seg 2 in 73 ms). Measured 3 minutes after the recorder spool finished draining (988 MB left, 200 uploads/min still running), so query-api was still competing with the upload backlog. n348 (pb_open_d1, 8,014 ms, 09:56) is the same window with both components visible: session_http 3,668 ms then 1,706 ms on the span60 open (catch-up), and a cold segment render of 3,307 ms on the day session (the rendition class seen all night). Recorded together because they are one condition, not two new kinds. CONFIRMED AND CLOSED by CV at 10:08 with their own measurement: five session creates on a real camera over 30-minute windows came back at 61, 149, 34, 71 and 24 ms — not merely inside the 50-750 ms all-night baseline but at its fast end — with query-api at 6.3 % CPU and timescaledb at 5.4 %, both idle, spool stable at ~940 MB. MECHANISM, theirs: session create is the DB-heavy half (build_manifest does four reads plus a Python walk) while segment serve is mostly file I/O, which is exactly why creates degraded to seconds while serves in the same runs stayed at 73-431 ms. So this was query-api and timescaledb competing with the 46 GB upload backlog, not a rendition cost and not a client defect
fix: none needed; normalised on its own once the backlog cleared, confirmed by measurement on both sides

cause: The 16-tile light-up took 6,497 ms against 2,705-4,028 ms for the seven earlier runs of this action. Not a client change (same build as the 2,828 ms run at 06:04) and not the backend incident (closed, CV measured session creates at 24-149 ms). The cause is the harness interfering with itself THROUGH THE BACKEND: soak actions run back-to-back as separate app launches, but the server-side work they start OUTLIVES the client process. n368 followed pb_churn at 10:15:29 and pb_smooth at 10:16:07, both playback-heavy; at 10:15-10:17 the host showed load 12-14 with io_full 13-19 % and reads to 200 MB/s, and playback-service was measured at 449 % CPU while the tabs run was lighting its wall. So a run's numbers can carry the tail of the previous run's server-side rendering. Sequential client launches are NOT sequential backend load.
fix: none applied - this is a property of the harness, not a defect to patch mid-run, and the driver's weighted-random ordering means it affects a minority of runs. Recorded so the report's outliers are read correctly: an isolated over-target on a UI or STARTUP action that follows a PLAYBACK or WALL action should be checked against the preceding row before it is attributed to the client. If this harness is run again, the cheap fix is a settle window between runs (poll the backend's CPU or simply wait ~30 s after playback-heavy actions) or grouping actions so heavy ones do not precede light ones; both cost wall-clock, which is why they were not added at 10:17 with 40 minutes left

cause: CV's close-out: the s3 gateway finished the night at 166 restarts, up from 140 mid-incident — about 26 more during recovery. It is stable now (15 min up, zero errors in five, 344 MiB of a 1 GiB cap, not OOM-killed), but the counter is the chronic condition from the 2026-08-30 s3 OOM-loop item and it climbed all through tonight.
fix: Not closed, recorded as a WATCH ITEM with a diagnostic shortcut that is the cheap lesson of tonight: IF UPLOADS START FAILING AGAIN, CHECK s3's RESTART COUNT BEFORE ASSUMING VOLUME SLOTS. Tonight's chain took about an hour to reach the -max=0 volume-slot ceiling, and an s3 restart loop produces the same visible symptom (PutObject InternalError, recorder spooling locally, disk filling). Two candidate causes, one cheap check, and checking it first costs nothing.
